title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 18: Lim v. Executive Secretary: Cases Are Not Decided on Hypothetical Assumptions
keywords: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
primary_topics: Chapter 18 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's account of Lim v. Executive Secretary, in which the Court by a 10-3 vote dismissed the challenge to the Balikatan exercise on procedural grounds, and of his own Separate Opinion insisting that cases cannot be decided on speculative or hypothetical assumptions.

His summary of the ponencia of Justice Sabino R. De Leon Jr. -- petitioners lacked taxpayer standing, certiorari and prohibition were improper remedies, the petition was premature and speculative, and though captioned otherwise it really sought declaratory relief, which the Court has no jurisdiction to give.

His report of the ponencia's substantive discussion of the VFA: the deliberate ambiguity of the word 'activities,' the resort to the Vienna Convention, the conclusion that combat-related activities as opposed to combat itself are authorized, and the Court's refusal to take judicial notice of media reports about what was happening in Mindanao.

His own position that the transcendental importance of the constitutionality question could have justified exempting the case from procedural requirements, but that the Petition simply lacked the factual moorings on which any intelligent disposition of the legal issues could rest -- so the nagging constitutional questions remain open for a properly presented case.
sub_topics: He sets the scene: American forces arriving in Mindanao to join Filipino counterparts in the Balikatan training exercise simulating the joint maneuvers contemplated under the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty, conducted in the shadow of the September 11 attacks.

He recounts the filing of the Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition directly with the Supreme Court by Arthur D. Lim, former president of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, and Paulino P. Ersando as citizens, lawyers and taxpayers, later joined by the militant party-list intervenors Sanlakas and Partido ng Manggagawa.

He states the petitioners' theory: the Mutual Defense Treaty allows military assistance 'only in case of an armed attack by an external aggressor,' and the VFA does not authorize American soldiers to engage in combat operations on Philippine territory.

He lists the four procedural grounds of dismissal: no taxpayer standing since Balikatan does not involve Congress's taxing or spending power; certiorari and prohibition improper for want of alleged facts showing grave abuse; prematurity because the claimed violation is speculative rather than actual or imminent; and the petition being in substance one for declaratory relief seeking advice, which the Court cannot give.

He notes that Justice de Leon nonetheless discussed the VFA, quoting the ponencia that the treaty's terminology is itself the source of the problem, that 'activities' was left undefined and ambiguous, and that the only limit is negative -- abstention from anything inconsistent with the agreement's spirit and from political activity.

He quotes the ponencia's view that the ambiguity was deliberate, giving both parties leeway, so that joint exercises may include patrol and surveillance training, sea search-and-rescue, disaster relief, school-building, and medical and humanitarian missions.

He quotes the conclusion that the VFA gives legitimacy to Balikatan, since mutual anti-terrorism advising, assisting and training falls under sanctioned activities, and that both the history and intent of the MDT and the VFA support authorizing combat-related activities as opposed to combat itself.

He reports that the Decision held US forces prohibited from engaging in an offensive war on Philippine territory, but that on the Petition's allegations the Court could not determine whether the troops were in fact so engaged.

He quotes the ponencia's refusal to take judicial notice of saturation media coverage, since facts must be established under the rules of evidence, and its refusal to accept without concrete proof the charge that the government was engaged in 'doublespeak.'

He quotes the ponencia's holding that the question is basically one of fact, unfit for a special civil action for certiorari whose sole object is to correct errors of jurisdiction or grave abuse -- a phrase of precise meaning denoting abuse 'too patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty.'
He notes that because the Court is not a trier of facts, the case was dismissed without prejudice to a new and sufficient petition in the proper Regional Trial Court.

He explains why he wrote separately: the transcendental importance of the constitutionality of Balikatan could have justified tackling the merits to put the legality of this major event to rest, but the Petition did not present enough factual moorings for an intelligent discussion.

He specifies the factual issues the Court could not decide -- whether US forces were actually engaging the Abu Sayyaf in combat and whether they would stay permanently -- and notes the Court has no authority to conduct a trial to establish such antecedents.

He quotes the petitioners' own averment that high-tech-armed Americans disguised as trainers would go to the war zones of Basilan and that 'A shooting war, not just an exercise, is unavoidable,' and answers that this is conjectural and unsupported by solid factual moorings.

He sets against it the Solicitor General's assurance that the Terms of Reference approved by both governments limit the exercise to no more than six months and prohibit American participants from combat, without prejudice to self-defense.

He states his rule of decision: cases cannot rest on assumptions of the form 'If the facts were these, then our decision would be this,' and courts may not consider facts unless alleged in the pleadings and proven, the Court's duty being to apply law to facts no longer in dispute.

He concludes that absent firm findings that the Americans will stay indefinitely or are engaged in actual offensive combat, grave abuse of discretion cannot be imputed to the officials hosting Balikatan -- an indispensable element of certiorari.

He lists five genuine questions that may yet be raised: whether the Abu Sayyaf are international terrorists threatening international peace; whether there is an external armed attack justifying invocation of the MDT; whether the deployment's size, kind and location fit the VFA's 'activities'; whether the real objective is rescuing the American hostages Martin and Gracia Burnham; and whether Balikatan poses a political question beyond the Court's authority.

He summarizes Justice Kapunan's dissent: no treaty of the kind Section 25 requires exists; the ASG's terrorism is not shown to be an external armed attack; the VFA cannot cover armed confrontation with what appear to be local bandits engaged in kidnapping and murder, which are police and domestic law-and-order matters; a single sniper's bullet could trigger massive US retaliation; and there are indications the US intends a more enduring presence.

He explains that his Separate Opinion did not refute Kapunan's points precisely because the Petition offered no factual bases for discussing the merits, and stresses that the Decision left the door open through a new action, with the substantive constitutional issues still unsettled.

stances.claim: The Petition failed because it lacked factual moorings: it never even alleged that American troops had been unconstitutionally engaged in actual offensive combat, and its claim that a shooting war was unavoidable was conjectural.

stances.claim: The substantive constitutional questions about Balikatan remain open and unsettled, and may be raised in an appropriate court once a petition sufficient in form and substance is presented.
stances.rhetorical_move: listing five 'nagging questions' left unanswered, and reading the dismissal as without prejudice rather than as vindication

stances.claim: The exercise is unconstitutional: no treaty of the kind Section 25 requires exists, the ASG's acts are not an external armed attack, the VFA cannot cover suppression of local bandits, and the American presence is counterproductive and possibly enduring.

notable_anecdotes: Writing separately under constraint: he says he agreed the case should be dismissed but 'was constrained to write a Separate Opinion' to explain what the Petition lacked.

The shooting-war allegation: he quotes the petitioners' vivid claim that American soldiers 'disguised as trainers or advisers' would go to the war zones of Basilan and base themselves in the Sampinit complex, making a shooting war unavoidable.

The Court refusing the television: he records the ponencia's refusal to take judicial notice of the saturation media coverage of events 'down south,' since facts must be established under the rules of evidence.
The five nagging questions: he sets out the unanswered issues, including whether the real American objective was the rescue of the hostages Martin and Gracia Burnham.
The sniper's bullet: he reports Kapunan's warning that a single ASG sniper felling an American soldier could be used as an excuse for massive retaliation by US ground and air forces.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' recounted Lim v. Executive Secretary, the challenge to the Balikatan joint military exercise brought directly to the Supreme Court by Arthur D. Lim, a former president of the Integrated Bar, and Paulino P. Ersando as citizens, lawyers and taxpayers, joined by the party-list intervenors Sanlakas and Partido ng Manggagawa. The petitioners argued that the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty permitted assistance only against an armed attack by an external aggressor and that the Visiting Forces Agreement did not authorize American combat operations on Philippine soil. By 10 to 3 the Court, through Justice Sabino R. De Leon Jr., dismissed the Petition on procedural grounds: no taxpayer standing, certiorari and prohibition being improper remedies on the facts alleged, prematurity because the claimed violation was merely speculative, and the Petition being in substance one for declaratory relief, which the Court has no jurisdiction to grant. The ponencia nonetheless discussed the VFA's deliberately ambiguous term 'activities,' concluded that combat-related activities as distinguished from combat itself were authorized, refused to take judicial notice of media coverage of events in Mindanao, and dismissed the case without prejudice to a sufficient petition in the proper Regional Trial Court. CJP agreed with the dismissal but wrote separately. He acknowledged that the 'transcendental importance' of the constitutional question could have justified relaxing procedure, but held that the Petition lacked 'enough factual moorings upon which to base an intelligent discussion and disposition of the legal issues': it never alleged that American troops had actually engaged in offensive combat, and its claim that a shooting war was unavoidable was conjectural, set against the Solicitor General's Terms of Reference limiting the exercise to six months and barring combat. He stressed that cases could not be decided on hypothetical assumptions, that courts may consider only facts alleged and proven, and that without firm findings no grave abuse of discretion could be imputed. He listed five questions that remained genuinely open, summarized Justice Kapunan's dissent, and concluded that the substantive constitutional issues were still unsettled.
